name: Mercury skin lightening
lead: Mercury skin lightening refers to the use of creams, soaps and lotions containing mercury compounds to make the skin paler or to fade dark spots. The World Health Organization describes skin lightening as a dangerous practice often associated with exposure to mercury salts, which inhibit melanin production, and says mercury-containing lightening products are hazardous and have been banned in many countries [1].

Mercury and lead compounds have a long history in cosmetics: Wikipedia reports mercury was used as a lightening agent in ancient Greece and Rome, and that white women in 19th-century America used products containing toxic amounts of lead and mercury [2]. Today such products are still reported to be obtainable online and through informal channels, and some have been found to contain mercury without listing it as an ingredient [1][2].

Reported health effects of mercury exposure include kidney and neurological damage; it is not a treatment used in clinical dermatology. The sources contain no looksmaxxing forum discussion of mercury creams, and no clinical trials of mercury lightening exist among them.
infobox: Banned or restricted in many countries [1][2]

paras: The active ingredient is typically an inorganic mercury salt added to a cream or soap. Wikipedia notes that mercury accumulates in the dermis and that prolonged use can discolour the skin [2]. WHO states that mercury salts act by inhibiting melanin production [1].

Mercury was used as a lightening agent in ancient Greece and Rome, alongside white lead carbonate, and these products were known to erode skin [2]. In the 19th century, products containing toxic amounts of lead and mercury were used in the United States [2]. South Africa began regulating lightening products in the 1970s, banning those with mercury or high hydroquinone levels [2].

Wikipedia cites figures for use of lightening products in general, not mercury specifically: about 77% of women in Nigeria, 52% in Senegal and 25% in Mali in 2013, with roughly 40% in Asia [2]. Creams in Pakistan have been found to contain toxic levels of mercury and hydroquinone, and in 1997 French police dismantled a trafficking network in lightening products, mainly serving Congolese migrants; a Paris hospital created a specialist department for bleaching-related skin disorders [2]. UK trading standards have faced difficulty stopping illegal sales [2].

WHO reports that inorganic mercury salts are corrosive to skin, eyes and the gastrointestinal tract and may cause kidney toxicity if ingested; neurological and behavioural effects include tremors, insomnia, memory loss and headaches, and kidney effects range from protein in the urine to kidney failure [1]. A study by Mahé and colleagues described kidney damage and neurological effects, including insomnia, memory loss and irritability, in users of lightening products [2]. WHO has noted an association between inorganic mercury added to these products and skin cancer, according to Wikipedia [2].

Laboratory and toxicology reviews describe mercuric chloride as causing kidney injury, particularly in a specific segment of the proximal tubule, and as inducing autoimmunity in experimental animals; a 2025 review links mercury exposure to testicular degeneration and altered spermatogenesis in animal studies [3][4][5].

Some countries ban mercury in cosmetics while others still allow it [2]. WHO says mercury-containing lightening products have been banned in many countries and that it leads work to eliminate them [1]. The Minamata Convention on Mercury was adopted in 2013, and a 2023 amendment prohibits the manufacture, import or export of certain mercury-added products after 2025, a list that includes cosmetics [1].

No studies found. Research on mercury in lightening products consists of toxicology and case literature on mercury exposure in general, and none of the sources used here is a trial of mercury as a cosmetic lightening treatment.

timeline.event: South Africa begins regulating lightening products, banning mercury-containing and high-hydroquinone ones [2]

card.summary: Toxic mercury-salt lightening creams banned in many countries but still found in informal markets; no clinical use.
card.note: WHO describes mercury lightening products as hazardous; kidney and neurological damage are reported.

quick.overview:
Some skin-lightening creams and soaps contain mercury salts, which pale the skin by suppressing melanin. They have a long history, from ancient Rome to the 19th century, and remain sold in informal and online markets despite bans in many countries.

There are no clinical trials of mercury as a cosmetic treatment and no forum discussion in the sources reviewed; the literature is about toxicity.
quick.mechanism: Inorganic mercury inhibits melanin production and accumulates in the skin, which also can discolour it over time.
quick.risks: WHO describes these products as hazardous: kidney damage, tremor, insomnia, memory loss and headaches have been reported, and some products contain undeclared mercury. A 2023 Minamata Convention amendment bars manufacture, import and export of mercury-added cosmetics after 2025.
